research_study_list.full_text: DECOHERENCE IS AN ECHO OF ANDERSON LOCALIZATION IN OPEN QUANTUM SYSTEMS FREDERIK RAVN KLAUSEN AND SIMONE WARZEL Abstract. We study the time evolution of single-particle quantum states described by a Lindblad master equation with local terms. By means of a geometric resolvent equation derived for Lindblad generators, we establish a finite-volume-type criterion for the decay of the off-diagonal matrix elements in the position basis of the time-evolved or steady states. This criterion is shown to yield exponential decay for systems where the non-hermitian evolution is either gapped or strongly disordered. The gap exists for example whenever any level of local dephasing is present in the system. The result in the disordered case can be viewed as an extension of Anderson localization to open quantum systems. 1. Introduction Decoherence appears to be unavoidable in all quantum systems. The phenomenon is well de- scribed in the setting of local single-particle open quantum systems which have been the subject of extensive studies [46, 27, 16, 19, 25]. Such models found wide applications, including in biol- ogy, where they have been employed to understand dephasing-assisted transport [37]. We study the off-diagonal position matrix elements of quantum states, which are time-evolved under locally generated Lindblad dynamics. We prove exponential decay of these off-diagonals, which can be considered a statement of the lack of coherence of states in the position basis. The results transfer to the infinite-time limit, which means that we rigorously demonstrate that macroscopic superpo- sitions in the position basis are largely impossible as steady states. These findings have potential implications for collapse theories of quantum mechanics [21], and resource theories of coherence [7, 33]. The main technical result of this paper is a criterion for the decay of off-diagonal matrix elements in Lindbladian dynamics with local terms. The criterion is derived in analogy to finite-volume criteria in statistical mechanics and geometric resolvent equations in the theory of random Schr¨ odinger operators (cf. [3, 26]). Notably, our criterion only requires knowledge of the non-hermitian part of the Lindbladian, thus justifying the study of non-hermitian, maximally dissipative Hamiltonians. We present two applications of the criterion. First, we derive a Combes-Thomas estimate for non-normal operators to show that a uniform spectral gap in the non-hermitian Hamiltonian leads to exponential decay of matrix elements of the Abel-averaged state and steady states of the full Lindbladian, with constants independent of system size. This applies to systems with any level of dephasing dissipation – an implication, which is standard in the single qubit case (cf. [34, Ch. 8.4.1]), and which we generalize here. In the second application, we consider Lindbladians consisting of random operators with a dissi- pative part exhibiting a spectral gap that can close polynomially in system size. In this case, we establish exponential bounds for sufficiently large disorder. This result is motivated by the study of Anderson localization in open quantum systems [45, 42, 44, 41]. It is generally believed and proven in certain translation-covariant cases [12, 20] that the dynamics in disordered, open quantum sys- tems is diffusive – with a diffusion constant which depends on the disorder strength, but does not vanish even for large disorder. Single-particle Anderson localization in the dynamical sense [4, 3] Date: February 27, 2024. 1 arXiv:2310.09880v2  [math-ph]  24 Feb 20242 FREDERIK RAVN KLAUSEN AND SIMONE WARZEL therefore generically ceases to exist in open quantum systems. We point out that a lasting effect of the localization regime is the exponential decay of the off-diagonals of time-evolved states and steady states. The paper is organized into sections describing the setup, providing examples, deriving the decay criterion, discussing applications, and concluding with a discussion and outlook. The appendix contains supplementary material on spectra and resolvent estimates for maximally dissipative op- erators and the proof of the non-normal Combes-Thomas estimate. A previous and typographically substantially different version of this paper was part of the PhD thesis of the first author [26]. 2. Local Lindbladians and their Abel-averaged dynamics We consider single-particle open quantum systems described on a graph, which, for simplicity, is taken as a subset Λ ⊂ Zd of the d-dimensional lattice. The infinite-volume case Λ = Zd is allowed, but it is not the only case of interest. (Generalizations to other amenable graphs than Zd are rather straightforward.) Throughout, for two vertices x, y∈ Λ, we let d(x, y) denote the graph distance in Λ between x and y, and for Z ⊂ Λ we let diam(Z) be the diameter with respect to the distance d. The time evolution of quantum states ρ, i.e., non-negative elements of the Banach space of trace- class operators S1(ℓ2(Λ)) with trace Tr( ρ) = 1 on the Hilbert space ℓ2(Λ) of square summable complex-valued functions on Λ, will be Markovian, that is, modelled by a Lindblad master equation: ∂tρt = L(ρt), L(ρ) = −i[H, ρ] + D(ρ). For the semigroup exp (tL), t ≥ 0, to preserve the trace and non-negativity, a sufficient condition is that the dissipative term is of Lindblad form [22, 30] D(ρ) = X α  LαρL∗ α − 1 2(L∗ αLαρ + ρL∗ αLα)  . In quantum optics and numerical simulation of open quantum systems, the Lindbladian L is often split up into two parts [14, 32]: the non-hermitian evolution defined through the effective Hamiltonian H − i 2 X α L∗ αLα, (2.1) and the quantum jump term, which coincides with the first term in the sum over α in D. This split will emerge naturally in our geometric resolvent analysis. In order to define the Lindbladian mathematically properly as a bounded operator on S1(ℓ2(Λ)), we take all operators entering from the space of bounded operators B(ℓ2(Λ)). Both the self-adjoint Hamiltonian H = H∗ ∈ B(ℓ2(Λ)) as well as the operators ( Lα) ⊂ B(ℓ2(Λ)) are assumed to act locally in the canonical position orthonormal basis ( δx)x∈Λ of ℓ2(Λ) with an overall bound on the diameter of their supports. The support of an operator A ∈ B(ℓ2(Λ)) is taken to be supp(A) = {x ∈ Λ | ∃y ∈ Λ : ⟨δy, Aδx⟩ ̸= 0 or ⟨δx, Aδy⟩ ̸= 0}, where ⟨φ, ψ⟩ denotes the scalar product on ℓ2(Λ), which we define linear in its second component. The following formalizes the assumed locality. Assumption 2.1. We call a Lindbladian (R, I, N)-local (or short: local) on Λ with some R, I, N < ∞ if H = X Z⊂Λ hZ, D(ρ) = X Z⊂Λ DZ(ρ), DZ(ρ) = X α∈IZ  LαρL∗ α − 1 2(L∗ αLαρ + ρL∗ αLα)  , with hZ = h∗ Z, supp hZ = Z and supp Lα ⊂ Z for any α ∈ IZ and any Z ⊂ Λ. We suppose that all terms vanish, hZ = 0 and DZ = 0, for any Z ⊂ Λ with diam(Z) > R. Moreover, for any Z ⊂ Λ,DECOHERENCE IS AN ECHO OF ANDERSON LOCALIZATION IN OPEN QUANTUM SYSTEMS 3 the cardinality of the index set IZ is uniformly bounded, |IZ| ≤I, and the operator norm of all local terms is uniformly bounded, i.e., ∥hZ∥ ≤N and ∥Lα∥ ≤N for all α ∈ IZ, Z ⊂ Λ. We remark that constants in bounds in this paper will only depend on R, I, N, which are assumed to be independent of Λ ⊂ Zd (for fixed d). Under this assumption, such bounds are hence uniform in Λ. Proposition 2.2 (Quantum dynamical semigroup of contractions) . Under Assumption 2.1, L is the generator of a norm-continuous, positivity and trace preserving contraction semigroup exp(tL) on the Banach space S1(ℓ2(Λ)) of trace-class operators. The proof is spelled out in Appendix A. 2.1. Abel-averages and resolvents We investigate the long-term behavior and steady states of exp( tL). Steady states are the states in the kernel of the Lindbladian, ker L = {ρ ∈ S1(ℓ2(Λ)) | L(ρ) = 0 }. If Λ is finite, the relation between spectral properties of L and its long-term behavior is well-established and the existence of steady states is guaranteed [6]. However, the latter might be non-unique. E.g., in case D = 0 every eigenstate of H is a steady state. Our results will hold for any steady state, regardless of whether we have uniqueness or not. The time evolution exp( tL)(ρ) may lack a limit t → ∞for arbitrary initial states ρ. The time- averaged semigroup, such as the Abel average, Aε, ε >0, is better behaved for arbitrary initial state ρ, Aε(ϱ) = ε Z ∞ 0 e−tεetL(ρ) dt. (2.2) It represents an averaged evolution ofρ up to the timescaleε−1. Since exp (tL) maps states to states, Aε(ϱ) is a convex combination of states and therefore a state. By the Lumer-Phillips theorem [18, Thm. 3.15], as a generator of a contraction semigroup, L is a maximally dissipative operator on S1(ℓ2(Λ)). Hence, any ε >0 is in the resolvent set of L, and the Abel average can be expressed in terms of the resolvent: Aε(ρ) = ε (ε − L)−1(ρ). (2.3) In the infinite-time limit ε → 0, the state ρ gets projected to the kernel of L, i.e., the subspace of steady states: lim ε↓0 Aε(ρ) = Pker(L)(ρ). Our primary focus is to explore how the locality of the Lindbladian impacts the decay of off- diagonal matrix elements⟨δx, Aε(ρ)δy⟩, and consequently,⟨δx, ρδy⟩, for steady statesρ in the graph’s distance d(x, y). To motivate and highlight these results and their limitations, we provide several examples. 2.2. Examples: dephasing, dissipative engineering, and disorder The following examples fit our setup of local single-particle Lindbladians. They have been inves- tigated from a spectral point of view in one dimension in [27]. A simple example is the dissipation by local dephasing. Example 2.3. Local dephasing is defined through the Lindblad operators Lv = |δv⟩⟨δv| indexed by vertices v ∈ Λ of the graph, i.e., IZ = ∅ unless Z = {v}, where we set I{v} = {v}. If H = 0 , every pure position eigenstate |δv⟩⟨δv| is a steady state of L, and so is any linear combination. In particular, in case Λ is a finite subset, the maximally mixed state 1 1/|Λ| is a steady state, and remains so even if H ̸= 0.4 FREDERIK RAVN KLAUSEN AND SIMONE WARZEL We note that the maximally mixed state is always a steady state of any (local) Lindbladian on a finite graph in case the operators (Lα) are all normal (as is the case for dephasing Lindbladians). In such a case, our subsequent statements on the decay of off-diagonal matrix elements of this steady state are of course obsolete. Dissipative engineering is the idea of using carefully chosing dissipation as a method of preparing quantum states. In the many-body case, examples of coherent states prepared by dissipation are given in [43]. The following example of dissipative engineering was introduced in the many- body setting in [15] to describe how to construct states with desired coherence properties through dissipation. Its physical realization was implemented in [31]. Example 2.4. Coherence creation is defined through the Lindblad operators L(v,w) = (|δv⟩ + |δw⟩)(⟨δv| − ⟨δw|) . (2.4) indexed by the edges (v, w) ∈ EΛ of the graph associated with Λ ⊂ Zd, i.e., IZ = ∅ unless Z = {(v, w)} where (v, w) is an edge of the graph, i.e., d(v, w) = 1. These L(v,w) are not normal and 1 2 X (v,w)∈EΛ L∗ (v,w)L(v,w) = X (v,w)∈EΛ (|δv⟩ − |δw⟩)(⟨δv| − ⟨δw|) = −∆Λ (2.5) coincides with the (negative) graph Laplacian associated with Λ. A steady state of a system consisting solely of this dissipation (i.e. H = 0 ) in finite volume is the pure, maximally extended state |1⟩⟨1| with ⟨δx, 1⟩ = 1 / p |Λ| for all x ∈ Λ. Thus, these Lindblad operators actively create coherence in the system. As explained in [15, Sec. II.A] in the one-dimensional case Λ ⊂ Z, the operator L(v,w) can be thought of as a pumping process where (upon translating the setup to second quantization) the operator (⟨δv| − ⟨δw|) annihilates out-of- phase superpositions and then the term (|δv⟩ + |δw⟩) recreates in-phase superpositions. The following example, which is a variant of the last one, was studied in [27, 46]. Whether it has the maximally mixed state as its steady state depends on the boundary conditions in the natural one-dimensional setup. Example 2.5. Incoherent hopping is defined on an oriented graph Λ and one associates to each of the oriented edges e = (w → v) the operator Le = |δv⟩⟨δw|. In particular, for one-dimensional case [0, n] ⊂ Z the Lindblad terms are of the form Lk = |δk⟩⟨δk+1| with 0 ≤ k ≤ n − 1. In case the line graph is completed to a ring, then the maximally mixed state |Λ|−11 1is a steady state even if H ̸= 0. Otherwise this ceases to be the case. The example has similarities with an exclusion process, that, at least in the many-body case, gives examples of open quantum systems that do not have the maximally mixed state as the steady state (see e.g. [39]). As far as the unitary part of the time evolution is concerned, we are particularly interested in studying random Schr¨ odinger operators. This is in line with recent studies [45] in which the coher- ence creating dissipation of Example 2.4 was used in combination with an Anderson Hamiltonian in the unitary part to numerically demonstrate how steady states become localized under the in- fluence of disorder. The robustness of such a dissipative control of single-particle localization was investigated in [42], and [41] discusses the extension of this concept to many-body localization. Example 2.6. A standard example of a Hamiltonian H on ℓ2(Λ) satisfying the Assumptions 2.1 is the (negative) discrete Laplacian −∆Λ defined in (2.5), plus a multiplication operator, i,e. V |δx⟩ = ω(x) |δx⟩ for all x ∈ Λ, corresponding to a bounded potential ω : Λ → R.DECOHERENCE IS AN ECHO OF ANDERSON LOCALIZATION IN OPEN QUANTUM SYSTEMS 5 Central to our study is the notion of a random potential, where ω(x), x ∈ Zd, are independent and identically distributed. For any local (non-random) Hamiltonian H0, a random Schr¨ odinger operator with disordered with strength λ >0 is a Hamiltonian is of the form. H = H0 + λV. In case H0 is the negative discrete Laplacian, H is simply the Anderson model , introduced by Anderson [4] and since the subject of intense study (see e.g. [3] for mathematical results). Let us caution the reader that locality of L is not warranted in all physically sensible models. For example, the translation covariant dissipation studied in [23, 12, 20] does not fit the present set-up, since in these papers the Lindblad operators are defined in terms of finite linear combinations of the momentum basis. 2.3. Geometric resolvent equation and criterion for the decay of coherence We now return to the general set-up of local Lindbladians specified in Assumption 2.1 and discuss its implications with regard to bipartitioning Λ into two disjoint subsets Λ = Λ1 ⊎ Λ2. In such a bipartite geometry, we define a set of boundary sets as thoseZ ⊂ Λ with diameter smaller or equal to R, which intersect both sets: ∂ = {Z ⊂ Λ | diam(Z) ≤ R and Λj ∩ Z ̸= ∅ for both j = 1, 2}. We will also need a notion of a boundary of one of the subsets Λ j: ∂Λj = {Z ⊂ Λj | diam(Z) ≤ R and d(Z, Λ\Λj) ≤ R}, where d(Z, Z′) stands for the distance of the two sets Z, Z′ with respect to the graph distance on Zd. Comments on the finite-volume criterion Proposition 2.10 reduces investigations of the off-diagonal of an Abel-averaged, time-evolved quan- tum state – potentially in infinite-volume – to a computation of a finite-volume quantitykε x,y, whose length scale is defined via d(x, y). Concluding remarks We have identified two mechanisms for the exponential decay of the matrix elements of steady states of local Lindbladians L: a uniform spectral gap or Anderson localization in the non-hermitian Hamiltonian associated with L. Although these mechanisms have different physical origins, their resulting bounds are similar. In Section 3.3, we relied on a spectral gap assumption on the non-hermitian Hamiltonian associated with the Lindbladian to prove results for random systems. Let us explore the relationship between such a spectral gap and the presence of dark states of the Lindbladian. A dark state |ψ⟩ is defined by Lα |ψ⟩ = 0 for all α, and H |ψ⟩ = E |ψ⟩ for some E ∈ R. Dark states lead to steady states since L(|ψ⟩⟨ψ|) = 0. In the case of coherence creation in Example 2.4 (with H = 0), the uniform state |1⟩ is a dark state. Regarding the gap assumption, we note the following: • Only dark states can give rise to spectrum of the non-hermitian Hamiltonian associated with L on the imaginary axis. This can be demonstrated as follows. Let |ψ⟩ be an eigenvector of the non-hermitian evolution with eigenvalue z on the imaginary axis, then, 0 = Re(z) = Re(i⟨ψ, Hψ⟩ −1 2 X α ⟨ψ, L∗ αLαψ⟩) = −1 2 X α ∥Lα |ψ⟩∥2. In particular, |ψ⟩ must be an eigenstate of H, and hence a dark state. These considerations hold also true in a similar spirit for eigenvalues with small Re( z).16 FREDERIK RAVN KLAUSEN AND SIMONE WARZEL • For non-hermitian Hamiltonians with random potentials, it is unlikely that the eigenstates are approximately dark. This situation resembles a Lifshitz tail behavior for the spectrum near the imaginary axis, suggesting that a probabilistic estimate might replace the use of the gap assumption in the proof of Proposition 3.4. Extending these results and methods from single-particle systems to many-particle systems with interactions is an interesting challenge. Several of the cases we studied were the one-particle sector of many-body quantum systems with particle number preserving dissipation. In such cases, one can study each n-particle sector separately. This in particular applies to the study of random many-body systems such as in [41], where the localization properties with Lindblad operators as in Example 2.4 were investigated numerically. Methods from [2, 8, 17] could provide insights for this approach. Considering the many-particle case is intriguing even in the absence of disorder. We believe that the methods used here can be lifted to the many-particle sector, albeit with the constants scaling with the number of particles in the system. In addition, we caution the reader that coherence and correlation are even more dissimilar for many-particle systems than in the single-particle case we have studied in this paper. The results in this paper are reminiscent of theorems linking Lindbladian spectral gaps to correlation clustering [11, 24]. These works, however, operate in the many-particle setting and assume the Lindbladian possesses a unique, full-rank stationary state, which defines a Hilbert space for spectral analysis. Their methods differ substantially and rely on quantum analogs of classical techniques related to logarithmic Sobolev inequalities. It is noteworthy that the rela- tionship between spectral gaps, their behavior in infinite volume, and time-dependent decoherence has also been explored in previous studies of the single-particle case [10, 27]. llm_extracted_info.main_contributions: Studies decoherence (decay of off-diagonal position-basis density-matrix elements) for single-particle open quantum systems with local Lindblad generators on (subsets of) Z^d. Main contribution is a finite-volume-type criterion (via a geometric resolvent equation for Lindblad generators) that bounds off-diagonal elements of Abel-averaged states and steady states in terms of resolvents of an associated non-Hermitian, maximally dissipative “effective Hamiltonian” (the non-Hermitian part of the Lindbladian). Shows this criterion yields exponential decay in two regimes: (i) when the non-Hermitian evolution has a uniform spectral gap (e.g., any nonzero local dephasing), giving size-independent constants; (ii) when the system is strongly disordered, extending Anderson-localization-style exponential resolvent decay to open systems and implying exponential suppression of coherence even though transport/densities may remain diffusive.
llm_extracted_info.methodology: Defines (R,I,N)-local Lindbladians with bounded-range local Hamiltonian and Lindblad terms. Uses Abel averaging A_ε=ε(ε−L)^{-1} to connect long-time behavior to resolvents of the Lindbladian. Introduces bipartitions and admissible boundary Lindbladians to decouple regions and derive a geometric resolvent identity: (ε−L_0)^{-1} on off-diagonal blocks admits a contour integral over products of resolvents of maximally dissipative operators D_{Λx}, D_{Λy}. Establishes Proposition 2.10: off-diagonal coherence is controlled by an ‘associated kernel’ built only from resolvents of D operators plus boundary error terms. Provides tools to bound kernels: (a) a Combes–Thomas-type estimate extended to non-normal operators via pseudospectrum control, yielding exponential resolvent decay under a gap condition on −Re D; (b) fractional-moment method for non-Hermitian (dissipative) Anderson-type operators, giving exponential decay in expectation at strong disorder; combines independence-at-distance with Hölder/power-splitting to control contour integrals.
llm_extracted_info.experimental_setup: No numerical/empirical experiments; work is rigorous mathematical analysis. ‘Validation’ is via theorems and proofs applied to representative model classes: local dephasing (Lv=|v><v|), coherence-creating dissipation (L(v,w)=(|v>+|w>)(<v|−<w|)), incoherent hopping (Le=|v><w| on oriented edges), and random Schrödinger/Anderson Hamiltonians H=H0+λV with i.i.d. bounded-density onsite disorder. Benchmarks consist of proving exponential bounds for (i) uniformly gapped non-Hermitian evolution (Assumption 3.1) and (ii) strong-disorder fractional-moment localization for dissipative Anderson models (Theorem 3.6), leading to exponential decay of off-diagonal elements of Abel-averaged states and steady states; includes discussion of boundary vs bulk geometries and boundary-condition engineering through boundary Lindbladians.
llm_extracted_info.limitations: Restricted to single-particle (one-body) Lindblad dynamics on lattice graphs with bounded-range, bounded-norm local terms; excludes common translation-covariant dissipators defined in momentum space. Results focus on decay of off-diagonal position matrix elements (coherence) and do not imply dynamical localization of densities/transport; open systems may still be diffusive. Strongest deterministic decay requires a uniform spectral gap in −Re D (Assumption 3.1), which fails for models with dark states or Laplacian-type dissipators unless boundary conditions are modified; in disordered case, exponential bounds are typically in expectation and rely on independence-at-distance and strong disorder (fractional-moment localization). Kernel bounds can depend sensitively on boundary conditions; points near physical boundaries may require modified geometry/distances. Infinite-volume steady states may not exist, making steady-state statements conditional.
llm_extracted_info.future_research_directions: Replace explicit gap assumptions with probabilistic estimates near the imaginary axis (e.g., Lifshitz-tail-type bounds for small Re z) to treat dark/near-dark states in random settings more naturally. Extend the geometric resolvent criterion from single-particle to interacting many-body open systems and higher particle-number sectors, quantifying how constants scale with particle number and exploring connections to many-body localization under Lindblad dynamics. Develop analogous criteria for non-local/translation-covariant dissipators and more general graphs. Strengthen results from expected-value bounds to high-probability or almost-sure statements and investigate time-dependent (non-Abel-averaged) coherence decay rates. Explore links between non-Hermitian skin effects/boundary sensitivity and coherence decay criteria, potentially optimizing boundary Lindbladians for state engineering.

research_study_list.full_text: Learning Visual Tracking and Reaching with Deep Reinforcement Learning on a UR10e Robotic Arm Colin Bellinger Digital Technologies, National Research Council of Canada colin.bellinger@nrc-cnrc.gc.ca Laurence Lamarche-Cliche Software Engineering, Carleton University LaurenceLamarcheClic@cmail.carleton.ca Abstract As technology progresses, industrial and scientific robots are increasingly being used in diverse settings. In many cases, however, programming the robot to perform such tasks is technically com- plex and costly. To maximize the utility of robots in industrial and scientific settings, they require the ability to quickly shift from one task to another. Reinforcement learning algorithms provide the potential to enable robots to learn optimal solutions to complete new tasks without directly repro- gramming them. The current state-of-the-art in reinforcement learning, however, generally relies on fast simulations and parallelization to achieve optimal performance. These are often not possible in robotics applications. Thus, a significant amount of research is required to facilitate the efficient and safe, training and deployment of industrial and scientific reinforcement learning robots. This technical report outlines our initial research into the application of deep reinforcement learning on an industrial UR10e robot. The report describes the reinforcement learning environments created to facilitate policy learning with the UR10e, a robotic arm from Universal Robots, and presents our initial results in training deep Q-learning and proximal policy optimization agents on the de- veloped reinforcement learning environments. Our results show that proximal policy optimization learns a better, more stable policy with less data than deep Q-learning. The corresponding code for this work is available at https://github.com/cbellinger27/bendRL_reacher_tracker 1 Introduction Motivated by increasing labour costs and potential improvements in efficiency, a wide variety of scien- tific laboratories and industries have adopted the use of robotic arms for production, maintenance and service [BDCSTS21]. Robots are often ideal for repetitive, strenuous, and complex tasks that require speed and precision. To achieve this, however, the current generation of industrial and scientific I robots require manual programming by robotics engineers. The programmer uses motion planning based on forward and inverse kinematics, where forward kinematics combine the direct measurement of all joint orientations with the lengths of linkages connected to the joints to determine the end-effector position and inverse kinematics establish the values of joint positions required to place the end-effector at a new location with a new orientation. To make the incorporation of industrial robots more inclusive, modern systems enable skilled operators to manual manipulation of the robot via a control pendant. Although this can simplify the process, online manipulation via the control pendant presents its own challenges and limitations [LQK21]. Small and medium-sized institutions face additional barriers to the incorporation of robotic arms related to the cost of implementation and reprogramming the robot to handle evolving requirements [PNA +16]. Reinforcement learning (RL) is a form of machine learning, which is applicable to sequential decision-making problems, such as navigating [CFFF19], control [YM22], complex games [SHS +18], 1 arXiv:2308.14652v1  [cs.AI]  28 Aug 2023etc. With RL, the agent learns a control policy to complete a task or achieve some goal. Importantly, the learning setup does not require supervised learning and the task can evolve or be adapted as requirements and environments change. As a result, RL offers a general alternative to task-specific robot programming with the potential to simplify the adoption of industrial robots. On the other hand, many challenges exist in the applications of RL to real-world robotics. These include the re- quirement to ensure the safety of the robot and surroundings during learning, the need to define a reward function to effectively direct policy learning, and potentially long training times [SBS +18]. Figure 1: UR10e Robot used in this work. In this work, we evaluate the ability to learn image-based reaching and tracking asks via re- inforcement learning on the UR10e robotic arm by Universal Robots. The reaching and track- ing tasks considered here are inspired by pre- vious work in [YM22] with a UR5 robot. The UR10e robot used in this work is shown in Figure 1. In our experiments, we evaluate the poten- tial of the off-policy, value-based method Deep Q-Learning (DQN), and the on-policy, policy gradient method Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO). Our results show that PPO learns a bet- ter, more stable policy with less data than DQN. In order to improve its performance, DQN re- quires a more sophisticated exploration strategy and non-uniform sampling of its replay buffer to focus updates on the most informative experi- ence. 2 Background RL problems are formally described by a Markov decision process (MDP). An MDP is defined by the tuple (S, A, P, R, γ), where S and A are discrete or continuous action- and state-spaces, P is the state transition dynamic which map state-action pairs at time t onto a distribution over next states at time t + 1, R is a reward function that emits an instantaneous reward at time t + 1 given the state-action pair at time t, and γ ∈ [0, 1) is a discount factor that balances the importance of immediate versus future rewards. Setting γ closer to 0 place greater importance on rewards accumulated in the near- term. In RL, P and R are unknown to the agent. The states under the MDP setup satisfy the Markov Property, which dictates that the future is conditionally independent of the past given the present state. If this property does not hold, then the learner faces a partially observable Markov decision process (POMDP). In addition to the elements of the MDP, A POMDP contains an observation space Ω, which alone is not sufficiently informative to select the next action, and a state-action observation probability function O(ot+1|at, st+1). When RL is applied to POMDPs, Ω and O are also unknown to the agent. The agent receives an observation at each time step, t, rather than the underlying state of the system. Image-based RL applications are often partially observable because a single image is not sufficient to encode the dynamics of the world and other details that are relevant to action selection. In deep RL, POMDPs are typically handle with a combination of stacking a sufficiently long history of state-action pairs, a state encoder and/or a recurrent neural network [IZL +18]. In RL, the agent learns a policy,π, through sequential interactions with the environment (the world outside of the agent). At each time step, the policy maps the state to an action or distribution over actions π : st → at. The sequence of states, actions and rewards, ( s0, a0, r1, s1, a1, r2, s2, ...) under a policy π is denoted a trajectory or roll-out. The agent’s objective is to learn a policy π∗ that maximizes the return, G, π∗ = arg max π E[G|π]. (1) 2The return, G, is defined as: Gt = t=T−1X t=0 = γtrt+1, (2) where T is the length of a finite horizon MDP, or ∞ for an infinite horizon MDPs. In the case of infinite horizons γ ∈ [0, 1). For more details see [SB18]. 3 Related Work 3.1 Reinforcement Learning In recent years, the combination of reinforcement learning with deep feature learning has produced impressive advancements in the field of RL. Some noteworthy successes in deep RL include agents learning to play Atari 2600 video games directly from images [MKS +15], learning to play and defeat the world champion of Go [SHM +16], and learning to cool large industrial buildings [LPV +22]. Deep Q-Learning (DQN) provided an early breakthrough in deep reinforcement learning [MKS+13]. It was the first deep RL algorithm capable of effectively learning directly from raw visual inputs. DQN is a value-based, off-policy RL algorithm that is suitable for discrete action spaces and discrete or continuous state spaces. DQN utilizes a deep neural network as its state-action value function ( Q- function). More specifically, given a state st, the neural network Q-function predicts the value of taking each possible action a ∈ A in st, where the value approximates the expected return starting from st, taking the action a, and thereafter following policy π. During training, the agent interacts with the environment according to an ϵ-greedy policy. Specifically, 1 −ϵ percent of the time, the agent selects an action according to its current policy, and ϵ percent of the time the agent selects a random action. The aim is to gain experience whilst balancing the exploration-exploitation trade-off. Tuples of experience are recorded in a fixed-length experience replay buffer and used to update the Q-function according to the objective: Li(θi) = E(s,a,r,s′)  yi − Q(s, a; θi) 2 (3) with yi = r + γ max a′ Q(s′, a′; θ−), (4) where θ is the Q network parameters, θ− is the target network parameters and i is the current iteration of network updates. The parameters of the target network are copied from the Q network every τ step or slowly shifted towards θ using soft Polyak updating. This, along with the use of the replay buffer, improves the stability of the deep Q network. Other improvements to DQN include Double Q-Learning, which improves DQN’s overestimation action values under certain conditions [VHGS16] and Dueling DQN which generalizes learning across actions leading to better policy evaluation in the presence of many similar-valued actions [WSH +16], and prioritize experience replay which improves learning by replaying important transitions more frequently [SQAS15]. A key advantage of off-policy methods, such as DQN, is sample efficiency. In comparison to on-policy methods, off-policy methods gain sample efficiency through the reuse of data collected under previous versions of the policy and the option to curate training batches such that experiences that produced more reward in the past are seen more frequently during training. Proximal Policy Optimisation (PPO) is a policy gradient form of RL algorithm that has many of the advantages of its predecessor, Trust Region Policy Optimization (TRPO), but is easier to implement, more general, and has better sample efficiency [SWD +17]. Unlike DQN, PPO is suitable for discrete or continuous state- and action- spaces. A key feature of PPO is the use of clipping in the objective function to reduce the risk of large policy updates that lead to a collapse in performance. Policy updates in PPO are conducted in an on-policy manner by collecting experience roll-outs under the 3current parameterized policy πθi and updating the policy as: θi+1 = arg max θ Es,a∼πθi  L(s, a, θi, θ)  (5) using stochastic gradient ascent. The loss, L is: L(s, a, θi, θ) = min πθ(a|s) πθi(a|a) Aπ θi(s, a), clip �πθ(a|s) πθi(a|a) , 1 − ϵ, 1 + ϵ  Aπ θi(s, a)  , (6) where A is an estimate of the advantage function, which measures whether or not an action is better than the policy’s default behaviour, and ϵ is a small hyper-parameter that controls the maximum step size of the policy update. A key advantage of PPO over many other RL algorithms is its robustness under a wide range of hyper-parameters. Particularly in comparison with DQN, PPO can require significantly less hyper-parameter tuning. This is a beneficial feature for many RL applications, such as robotics. Soft Actor Critic (SAC) is an off-policy algorithm that is suitable for continuous state- and action- spaces [HZAL18]. In addition, there is a variation applicable to discrete action-spaces [Chr19]. SAC learns a stochastic policy that is trained to maximize the expected return with entropy regularization. In particular, it learns a parameterized policy πθ and Q-networks Qϕ1 and Qϕ2 . SAC uses the clipped double-Q trick and takes the minimum Q-value of Qϕ1 and Qϕ2 for use in the loss function: L(ϕi, D) = E(s,a,r,s′,d)∼D  Qϕi(s, a) − y(r, s′, d) 2 , (7) where D is the replay buffer, d indicates if s′ is terminal, and: y(r, s′, d) = r + γ(1 − d)  min Qϕtarget,j (s′, ˜a′) − αlogπθ(˜a′|s′)  , ˜a′ ∼ πθ(·|s′), (8) where α controls the explore-exploit trade-off. The α value is the main hyperparameter that should be tuned in SAC. A larger α encourages more exploration. The policy network, πθ, acts to maximize the expected future return plus expected future entropy. In this way, both future rewards and exploration are encouraged. In particular, SAC learns to maximize: V π(s) = Ea∼π  Qπ(s, a)  + αH(π(·|s)), (9) where H(·) is entropy. In practice, this is optimized using the reparameterization trick where a sample is drawn from πθ(·|s) by computing a deterministic function of state, policy parameters, and independent noise. In addition to the sample efficiency that comes with off-policy learning, SAC has the advantage of being relatively insensitive to hyperparameters and balances the exploration-exploitation trade-off through the use of entropy regularization. 3.2 Reinforcement Learning with Physical Robots Advancements in RL and the reduced costs of some robotics systems have resulted in a significant increase in the number of RL researchers working on robotics applications. This includes, for ex- ample, object manipulations skills, [GHLL17, HZAL18], peg insertion [LZS +19], targeted throwing [GMKB17], and dexterous manipulation [ZGR +19]. Nonetheless, many significant challenges remain for the widespread application of RL to robotics. These include issues such as image observation and multi-format observation, sample efficiency, sim-to-real training, human-free learning, including safe and reset-free learning, generalization across tasks, and learning in the open world. In relation to this work, there have been a few other applications of RL to versions of Universal Robots’ UR cobotic arms. This work takes direct inspiration from Yufeng and Mahmood [MKKB18, YM22] work on asynchronous RL for real-time control. Yufeng and Mahmood trained SAC RL to control a UR5 robot to complete reaching and tracking tasks. In their experimental setup, the target 4is rendered on a computer monitor in front of the robot. Rendering the target on a computer monitor has many practical advantages, such as safe and reset-free learning, whilst maintaining some important real-world robotics challenges. The state-space in this setup is composed of visual inputs from a camera mounted on the end-effector and the joint position of the arm. The combination of images and joint information reduces the risk of partial observability. In [MTR +17], RL is applied to learn a control policy to enable a UR5 robot to complete the wire rope problem. The authors in [FTCG20], compared Trust Region Policy Optimization and Deep Q-Network with Normalized Advantage Functions to Deep Deterministic Policy Gradient and Vanilla Policy Gradient in simulation and with transfer to UR5. UR3e robots were the subject of RL learning the peg in the hole task in [BHPRAH20], pick and place in [GMLW22] and goal-based RL [PM21]. 4 RL Environment In the following experiments, a UR10e robot from Universal Robots learns to carry out reaching and tracking tasks from visual inputs. The inputs are captured by a Point Grey camera mounted on the end-effector of the robotic arm. Tracking and reaching are performed with respect to a digital target rendered on a 1920x1200 monitor fixed at a distance of 70 cm from the robot. The target is a red circle on a white background. The setup is shown in Figure 1. In order to obtain results that would transfer more easily to real-world applications, the background of the room is unobstructed and total light in the room can vary due to changes in the outdoor light through the North facing windows. The specifics of the physical reacher and tracker RL environment are described in the following sections. In both the reacher and tracker tasks, the robotic arm has a fixed start position at the beginning of each episode. In the reacher task, the target location can be set to fixed or be randomly reset at the beginning of each episode. Alternatively, in the tracker task, the target is initialized at the centre of the monitor at the beginning of each episode. The target slowly drifts in one of 4 coordinate directions out from the centre of the monitor at a rate of 3 pixels per RL time step. The drift direction of the target is uniformly sampled at the beginning of each episode. The monitor frame boundaries reflect the target by reversing the direction on one axis. 4.0.1 Action Space The UR10e robotic arm has 6 degrees of freedom (base, shoulder, elbow and 3 wrist joints). The action space is composed of 10 discrete actions. These rotate one of of 5 joints either clockwise or counterclockwise (the third wrist would only rotate the camera, and therefore it was not included in the action space). Each joint’s rotation actions are set proportionally to the size of the joint, with larger joints having slightly larger rotation actions. In particular, the base rotates 0.025 radians (rads), the shoulder and elbow rotate 0.02 rads, and wrists 1 and 2 rotate 0.015 rads. The agent selects one joint to move per time step in either the positive or negative direction from its current position. For safety purposes, prior to sending a selected action to the robot via the UR10e’s movej API command, the RL environment validates the outcome of the move. The validation checks if the move will cause the arm to move out of the defined Cartesian limits. If the action is deemed to violate the limits, the environment steps forward without the robot moving. 4.0.2 Dynamics of the Environment The environment is episodic. One time step in the environment includes one synchronous interaction between the agent and the environment. In particular, this involves: 1) the environment calculating the current observation and reward, 2) sending the observation and reward to the agent, 3) the agent selecting the next action, 4) the agent sending the action to the environment, and 5) the environment 5Figure 2: This figure displays the agent-environment-hardware interaction framework. commanding the appropriate move of the robot. The interaction framework is visually presented in Figure 2. Each episode starts the robotic arm in a fixed joint position within the Cartesian boundaries. The episode ends when the agent has achieved the goal. For training purposes, we truncated the episode after 150 time steps if the agent as not achieved the goal. If the agent selects an action that will trigger a protective stop due to a rotation or boundary limit, the action is not initiated. Thus, the agent remains in its current position and state does not change. An observation from this location is returned to the agent. All other actions cause the arm to move a predefined amount via the movej command. The camera observation is made after the move is completed. 4.0.3 Reward The goal in each task is for the agent to learn to move camera on the end of the robotic arm as close as possible to the target and centre the target in the camera frame. A shaped rewards schemes is evaluated for this purpose. Arrival at the goal is determined by the size and centering of the target in the current observation frame. Given the frame size of 400x300 and that the target is included in the observation, the maximum distance between the centre of the frame and the centre of the visible target is 250 pixels. The maximum radius of the target is 40 pixels and the minimum radius is 10 pixels. For the goal to be achieved, the target must have a radius greater than 30 pixels and be less than 70 pixels from the centre of the frame. In the shaped reward setting, the agent receives a reward of 20 for achieving the goal. A reward of -0.01 is given if the target is not in the frame. If the target is in the frame, but the goal has not been achieved, intermediate rewards between zero and one are given. The intermediate rewards are increased based on how centred the target is and how close the camera is to the target. These are calculated as: dist reward = −1 × dist to goal/max dist to goal (10) radius reward = (target radius − max radius)/(max radius − min radius) (11) reward = radius reward + dist reward (12) If the agent selects an action that will trigger a protective stop due to a rotation or boundary limit, 1 is subtracted from the reward in order to discourage the agent from hitting the limits. 6Split channels Threshold  channels Mask Image  processing - Find the radius of the circle - Find the distance from the centre of  the frame Calculate   reward  -  = -1 x (dist_to_goal/max_goal_dist) +   (radius - max_radius)/(max_radius - min_radius) Rt  Rt Figure 3: This figure displays the image processing steps to determine if the target is in the current frame, along with the size and location of the target if it is present. 4.0.4 Image Processing A significant challenge in RL with image observations is calculating the reward. In this setup, the reward is based on the size and centring of the target (red circle) in the image captured by the camera on the robotic arm. Therefore, in order to compute the reward at each time step, the environment uses image processing to determine if the target is in the current frame. If the target is in the frame, the environment determines the radius and location of the target to be used in the reward calculation discussed above. There are multiple approaches that could be used to detect and quantify the target circle. In this work, we use openCV’s HoughCircles function, which uses the Hough transform [DH72], to identify circles in the observation image at each time step. The sensitivity and specificity of circle detection are controlled by four hyperparameters. In the initial experiments, the HoughCircles function was optimized on raw image observations. The experimental setup includes many factors that can be expected in open-world robotics, such as variable lighting, background noise containing a mix of objects, textures and colours, and dynamically changing angles and distances between the camera and target. Each of these factors contributes to poor sensitivity and specificity with HoughCircles function. In addition, the background has circular objects that needed to be ignored during the target identification for reward calculation. Therefore, the RL algorithm must be robust to some reward signal noise. As a result, a multi-step process to simplify the image observation by removing background details is used. This serves to significantly reduce false positives in the reward calculation. The steps are presented in Figure 3. First, the observation image is split into its three component channels (red, green and blue). Each channel has a threshold applied which maps all pixels, except those with nearly total presence, to total absence. The result of this is that most background details are removed, and in the case of the blue and green channels, the target circle is also removed. This can be seen in the images after the thresholding step in the figure. Next, the thresheld blue and green channels are applied as masks to the thresheld red channel. The resulting red channel has nearly all of the background details removed, with the target clearly intact. The final steps are to apply the HoughCircles function and calculate the reward as described in the previous subsection. 75 Experimental Setup We assess the performance of PPO and DQN on the reacher and tracker environments 1. In each case, the agent is trained end-to-end from scratch. Each agent is evaluated over 3 independent trials. PPO is trained over 40k time steps and DQN is trained over 60k time steps using the same CNN architecture. DQN uses a replay buffer of 20k and linear decay in the ϵ value from 1 to 0.01. The results are graphically presented as the mean and standard error of reward per episode step. In addition, the steps per episode over the course of learning is plotted as an alternative perspective on performance. Fewer steps per episode indicate better performance. All of the experiments utilize a HP Z6 G4 Workstation including Intel Xeon(R) Silver 4214R CPU @ 2.40GHz × 48 with the Ubuntu 22.04 operating system. Universal robot UR10e is running the URSoftware version 5.12. Communication between the Linux desktop an the UR10e robot uses ur rtde 1.5.5 software2. 6 Results and Discussion Figure 4 includes the learning curves for DQN and PPO on each environment in terms of mean reward (left) and mean steps per episode (right). The plots show that both RL algorithms improve their policies over the course of training to increase the mean reward. After 40k steps, however, PPO has a much higher mean reward than DQN on all three tasks. After an additional 20k of training, DQN is approximately equivalent on reaching and tracking, and remains much worse than PPO (with 40k of training) on the static reaching task. This suggests that epsilon greedy exploration and uniform sampling from DQN’s replay buffer are likely causing slow learning. Thus alternative strategies are needed to improve exploration and focus policy updates on the most valuable experience. The episode length plots demonstrate if, and how quickly, the agents are able to achieve the goal on each task. The most striking result is that although the reward results show that DQN learns to focus on the target in the static reacher task, it fails to achieve the goal within the maximum episode length of 150 steps. Alternatively, PPO learns to achieve the goal in a mean of 110 steps and is still improving its policy when training was stopped. Given that PPO has superior performance, the remainder of the analysis focuses on it. In comparing the performance of PPO across the three environment types, the plots illustrate that the agents are best at the static reacher, where the target is always located at the centre of the monitor. Alternatively, the reacher environment, where the target is randomly re-positioned at the beginning of each episode, is the most challenging of the three environments. The tracker environment, which has the target start each episode at the centre of the monitor and slowly drifts away, falls between static reacher and reacher in terms of complexity for PPO. The ordering of performance is likely due to the fact that in static reacher and tracker, the target is always initialized in the same location. As a result, the agent can quickly learn the general area that it should move towards at the beginning of each episode. Alternatively, because the target is randomly positioned at the beginning of each reacher episode, the agent must search for and find the target before it can move it on the target. Due to the nature of on-policy learning, the agent may be biased to search areas where the target occurred in the more recent updates and slowly forget pasted experience. In terms of training time, the clock time is approximately 3:30 hours for each agent. Figures 5, 6 and 7 show 3 episodes of evaluation rollouts for PPO agents at the end of training on the static reacher, reacher and tracker environments. The roll-outs are depicted with two images captured on 5-second intervals. The embedded image is the observation received by the agent and the larger image is from a separate camera used to record the robot and the target. The left plots in each row depict the mean rewards on the tracking, reaching and static reaching environments. The right plots in each row present the number of steps per episode in each environment. each episode commences with the agent looking away from the target and the monitor. Within the first 5 seconds, the agent locates the target, and once located the agent begins to move towards the target whilst keeping the target as centered as possible in its field of view. This is easiest in the static reacher environment where the target is always in the same location, and most challenging in the reacher environment. In Figure 5, the pattern of the size and location of the target is very similar in each evaluation roll-out. This suggests that the PPO agent has learned a stable and robust policy. An additional sign of the agent’s efficacy on this task is that after just 20 seconds the target size is quite larger. Alternatively, in the reacher environment after 35 seconds the target still appears relatively small and sometimes poorly centered. More learning time is clearly needed to deal with the larger problem. Figure 7 highlights the fact that the complexity of the tracker environment is moderate compared to the static reacher and reacher. In particular, the agent consistently locates and centres the target within the first 5 seconds, similar to static reacher and unlike reacher, which sometimes takes more than 5 seconds (depending on the target location.) Although the target is typically centered after 35 seconds, it is not nearly as large as in the case of static reacher. This is attributed to the fact that the agent must learn to approach and centre the drifting target. The precision of the agent is also limited by size of the discrete movements in the environment. Once again, additional training time would allow for further policy refinements on this task. 6.1 Limitations and Challenges The implementation of the RL environment has some limitations, such as the synchronization of the agent and the environment. Moreover, from the agent’s perspective time advances in discrete steps. This simplifies the tracker tasks because the target only moves as fast as the agent can select actions. In subsequent versions of the environment, the target will drift at a rate that is independent of the agent’s action selection rate. As described above, for example, the agent faces a discrete action space that limits the movement of the robot at each time step to a single joint and a fixed step size. Subsequent versions of the environment will add the option to use a continuous action space. A continuous action space will provide numerous advantages, including the ability to learn a smooth control policy and 9Figure 5: This figure displays three policy roll-outs for PPO on the static reacher environment after training is completed. It demonstrates that the agent learned to find the target and then navigate toward the target while keeping the target centered in the field of view. Figure 6: This figure displays three policy roll-outs for PPO on the reacher environment after training is completed. It demonstrates that the agent learned to find the target and then navigate toward the target while keeping the target centered in the field of view. a wider choice of additional RL algorithms. Finally, the observation space is composed of one image captured by the camera on the end-effector of the robotic arm. A single image state space, however, may not include all of the information relevant to reacher and tracker tasks. In the case of tracker, for example, a single image does not provide information about which direction the target is moving. Thus, the problem can be considered partially observable [Kri16]. This can be handled by using the combined recent history of state (or states and actions) as the input to the agent’s policy [MKS +13], or deep partially observable RL algorithms [IZL +18]. In addition, the physical robot has limits on its joint positions. Based on image states alone, however, the agent may not have sufficient information to learn these limits. The subsequent implementation of the environment will include the option to include both the current image and joint position in the state space. Reward calculation from raw images is an open and challenging problem in RL. It will become relevant as more RL is trained in the real-world. In this work, the reward is defined based on the size and centering of the target in the frame. Unlike the previous work, the background in the image is complex, the lighting is inconsistent and the agent has the ability to look away from the monitor containing the target. As a result, image processing needs to be applied at each time step to determine 10Figure 7: This figure displays three policy roll-outs for PPO on the tracker environment after training is completed. It demonstrates that the agent learned to find the target and then navigate toward the target while keeping the target centered in the field of view. if a reward should be given. This represents additional computational resources and requires problem- specific engineering of the reward function. Moreover, due to the limitations of image processing under these conditions, the rewards issued to the agent are noisy thereby increasing the learning challenge. DRL algorithms suffer from poor sample efficiency [Yu18]. Sample inefficiency occurs in two con- texts: a) train RL policy from scratch requires the agent to collect a large number of experience tuples (state, action, reward, next state), and b) the agent must be trained from scratch multiple times in order to find the best hyper-parameters for the given task. During online training, the robot cannot be used for other productive tasks. Future work will explore strategies for better robot utilization and sample efficiency. Sample efficiency is improved with off-policy algorithms that allow for the reuse of experience [VHGS16], the prioritization of particularly rewarding experience[SQAS15], and the distribution of agent learning across multiple robots[GHLL17]. In this work, however, the sensitivity of DQN to hyper-parameters necessitated significantly more training time than PPO. More generally, sim-2-real offers the potential to initialize the RL via faster, lower-cost interactions with a simulated robot, and then refine the policy on the real-world robot [TZC +18, YTB+20]. Similarly, model-based RL can be used for on- and off-policy RL to improve sample efficiency [NYA +18, YCI+20]. Other improvements may stem from self-supervised learning to reduce the agent’s reliance on heavily engineered, problem-specific rewards [LPK +18, PG16, ITF+21] and the use of frame skipping and observation skipping to reduce observation and decision costs in predictable regions of the state space [LSR17, BCT23]. 7 Conclusion This work explored the potential of reinforcement learning algorithms to learn optimal control policies for vision-based reacher and tracker tasks with a UR10e robotic arm. We describe the experimental setting and results of online policy learning with DQN and PPO. Whereas much of the research on vision-based RL is undertaken in highly controlled settings, here we train the agents in a complex physical setting with variable light conditions. We find that in these conditions the image-based reward calculations can be very sensitive to the background and variable light leading to a noisy reward signal. Careful image processing prior to reward calculation is required to minimize the risk of noise that can harm policy learning. 11Our results show that proximal policy optimization learns a better, more stable policy with less data than deep Q-learning. In order to improve its performance, we expect that DQN requires a more sophisticated exploration strategy and non-uniform sampling of its replay buffer to focus updates on the most informative experience. Finally, we highlight general challenges and future directions for the study of reinforcement learning in vision-based open-world robotics as: i) reducing the reliance on heavily engineered, domain-dependent rewards, ii) lowering the dependence on computationally expensive image processing for reward calculation, and iii) improving the robustness to the potential for degraded learning due to a noisy reward signal resulting from imprecision in the imaged-based reward calculations. llm_extracted_info.main_contributions: Investigates feasibility of training deep RL directly on an industrial UR10e arm for vision-based reaching and visual target tracking with minimal reprogramming. Contributes (i) two real-robot RL environments (static reacher, randomized reacher, drifting-target tracker) using an end-effector camera and a monitor-rendered target; (ii) a practical, robust reward-computation pipeline for noisy real-world images via OpenCV preprocessing + Hough circle detection; (iii) an empirical comparison of DQN vs PPO in this setting, showing PPO learns more stable policies with fewer real-robot samples/time than DQN, while DQN struggles with exploration and uniform replay.
llm_extracted_info.methodology: Formulates tasks as episodic RL with image observations and discrete joint-step actions. Implements 10-action discrete control over 5 UR10e joints (± fixed radian increments) with safety validation against Cartesian limits before executing movej. Reward shaping combines target centering distance and apparent radius (proxy for distance-to-target) plus goal bonus; penalties for target missing and for invalid/protective-stop actions. Target detection for reward uses OpenCV: channel thresholding and masking to isolate red circle, then HoughCircles to estimate circle center/radius. Trains end-to-end CNN-based agents using Deep Q-Network (off-policy, ε-greedy, replay buffer, target network) and Proximal Policy Optimization (on-policy, clipped surrogate objective with advantage estimates).
llm_extracted_info.experimental_setup: Hardware: Universal Robots UR10e (URSoftware 5.12) with Point Grey camera mounted on end-effector; target rendered as red circle on white background on 1920x1200 monitor placed ~70 cm from robot. Environments: (1) static reacher (target fixed at monitor center), (2) reacher (target randomized each episode), (3) tracker (target starts centered, drifts 3 px/step in one of 4 directions with boundary reflection). Observation: single 400x300 RGB image from end-effector camera; reward computed online each step via image processing. Episode: fixed start pose; terminate on success (radius >30 px and within 70 px of center) or truncate at 150 steps. Training: PPO for 40k environment steps; DQN for 60k steps; 3 independent trials each; DQN replay buffer 20k with ε linearly decayed 1→0.01. Metrics: mean reward per episode step with standard error; mean steps per episode; qualitative rollout screenshots. Runtime: ~3.5 hours wall-clock per agent on HP Z6 G4 workstation (Xeon Silver 4214R, Ubuntu 22.04); robot communication via ur-rtde 1.5.5.
llm_extracted_info.limitations: Real-time synchronization yields discretized time; in tracker, target motion is tied to agent step rate, simplifying tracking compared to continuous-time drift. Discrete action space (single-joint, fixed step size) limits control precision and smoothness; may cap performance especially for tracking. Partial observability from single-frame image (no explicit target velocity; no joint-state info), and arm joint limits are not directly observable from vision alone. Reward depends on engineered vision pipeline (thresholding + HoughCircles) that is sensitive to lighting/background and can be noisy, adding variance and requiring task-specific tuning and compute. DQN underperforms due to simple ε-greedy exploration and uniform replay; also shows higher hyperparameter sensitivity, increasing real-robot training burden. Experiments limited to a simple 2D monitor target and small-scale training (40–60k steps), with no sim-to-real transfer, no comparison to other continuous-control/off-policy methods (e.g., SAC), and limited statistical evaluation (3 trials).
llm_extracted_info.future_research_directions: Decouple target dynamics from agent step rate for more realistic tracking; move toward continuous-time environments. Extend to continuous action spaces (joint velocities/torques or Cartesian control) enabling smoother policies and use of algorithms like SAC/TD3. Reduce partial observability by stacking frames, adding recurrent policies, and/or augmenting observations with proprioception (joint positions) as in prior UR5 work. Improve DQN-style learning via better exploration (e.g., parameter noise), prioritized/non-uniform replay, and other DQN variants (Double/Dueling). Increase sample efficiency and robot utilization via sim-to-real pretraining, model-based RL, asynchronous/distributed learning across multiple robots, and observation/action skipping. Replace heavily engineered rewards with self-supervised or learned visual representations/goal estimators; improve robustness to reward noise and reduce dependence on expensive per-step image processing (e.g., lightweight detectors or learned segmentation).

research_hypothesis.open_problems: Current prompt-only CoT/L2M improvements often rely on the same LLM to both generate and verify reasoning, creating correlated failure: the model can confidently “rubber-stamp” its own incorrect intermediate arithmetic or inconsistent subproblem decomposition. This makes verifier-scored reranking brittle, hard to trust, and socially risky when deployed (silent wrong answers that appear internally consistent). The key unmet need is a *prompt-only* CoT framework that (1) searches over alternative decompositions, but (2) grounds selection in a verification signal that is at least partially *model-independent* and automatically checkable in Python, without fine-tuning or expensive tools.
research_hypothesis.method:
Refined hypothesis: **Proof-Carrying Least-to-Most (PC-L2M)** — a prompt-only L2M variant where each candidate solution must carry an *auditable, executable calculation trail* that a Python script can verify. PC-L2M combines (a) decomposition diversity with (b) external, deterministic validation, mirroring a human “do the work, then check the math” habit.

Core idea:
1) **Plan diversity (as in DV-L2M):** sample N candidate decompositions (N=3–8).
2) **Proof-carrying solve (new):** for each decomposition, require a dual-output format:
   - a short natural-language trace (optional), and
   - a strict **CALC** section: a sequence of arithmetic expressions in a constrained, executable mini-language (Python-safe arithmetic only), plus variable assignments when needed.
   Example CALC lines: `x = 3*7`, `total = x + 12`, `answer = total/3`.
3) **Deterministic verification (new):** a Python checker parses CALC, safely evaluates it (AST-whitelisted), and validates:
   - all assignments are evaluable,
   - referenced variables are defined,
   - the computed `answer` matches the model’s `FINAL` output,
   - (optional) integer-ness constraints for GSM8K.
4) **Selection rule (new):**
   - Discard candidates that fail verification.
   - If multiple pass: choose via (i) majority vote over verified answers or (ii) highest “simplicity” (fewest CALC lines) as a bias toward human-like minimal solutions.
   - If none pass: fallback to self-consistency majority vote.

Novelty vs common CoT reranking/self-verification:
- Moves the verifier signal from *LLM self-judgment* to a *model-independent, executable* proof obligation (“proof-carrying rationale”), while staying prompt-only.
- Turns decomposition search into **constraint satisfaction**: only candidates whose intermediate computations are mechanically checkable are eligible.
- Produces an artifact (CALC) that is auditable for safety/accountability, increasing real-world trust without training or external theorem provers.
research_hypothesis.experimental_setup:
Models (prompt-only, no fine-tuning):
- Primary: a small open instruct model (e.g., `meta-llama/Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct` or similar available locally).

Datasets:
- GSM8K test (first 200 examples for quick validation)
- SVAMP test (optional, first 200) for robustness to schema/wording changes

Baselines (all prompt-only):
1) Standard CoT (single sample)
2) Least-to-Most (single decomposition)
3) Self-Consistency CoT (K samples + majority vote)
4) DV-L2M (multi-decomposition + LLM scalar verifier; as in current hypothesis)

Proposed:
5) **PC-L2M** (multi-decomposition + proof-carrying CALC + Python verification + verified voting)

Protocol:
- For each question, run each method with fixed generation budget (max_new_tokens) and seeds.
- For self-consistency and multi-decomposition methods use comparable total sample counts (e.g., K=5, N=5).

Metrics to report:
- Primary: exact-match **accuracy** on final numeric answer.
- Secondary diagnostics (not for GAP): verification pass rate, fraction of questions where at least one candidate verifies, and average CALC length (proxy for “human-like minimality”).

Feasibility:
- Entire evaluation is a single Python script; verification uses only Python AST parsing.
- Runtime is manageable because verification is local and cheap (no extra LLM calls).
research_hypothesis.expected_result:
On GSM8K (first 200 test problems) with a ~1B instruct model and comparable sampling budgets:
- Standard CoT (1 sample): accuracy ≈ 0.45
- Least-to-Most (1 decomposition): accuracy ≈ 0.47
- Self-Consistency CoT (K=5): accuracy ≈ 0.49
- DV-L2M (N=5 + LLM verifier): accuracy ≈ 0.52
- **PC-L2M (N=5 + Python-verified CALC + verified vote): accuracy ≈ 0.55–0.58**

Secondary expectations:
- Verification pass rate: ~55–75% of candidates produce parsable CALC; among those, ~70–90% pass the arithmetic check (model-dependent).
- When at least one verified candidate exists, conditional accuracy is substantially higher (e.g., +10–20 points vs unconditional), indicating the verifier is selecting genuinely better solutions.

Interpretation: higher accuracy is better. PC-L2M’s gains come primarily from filtering out arithmetic/consistency errors that LLM self-verifiers frequently miss.
research_hypothesis.expected_conclusion: Prompt-only reasoning can be made meaningfully more reliable by requiring **proof-carrying** solution traces that are *mechanically checkable* in Python and using that check as the selection criterion over multiple decompositions. Compared to DV-L2M, PC-L2M is more novel and socially valuable because it reduces correlated self-verification failures (the model grading its own work) and produces auditable artifacts that support accountability. Academically, it reframes CoT improvement as a lightweight, training-free form of constraint-based inference; practically, it offers a drop-in reliability boost for low-cost models without fine-tuning or heavy experiments.

experimental_design.experiment_summary:
Goal: improve *final-answer correctness* on grade-school arithmetic word problems by reducing correlated self-verification failures in prompt-only Chain-of-Thought (CoT) / Least-to-Most (L2M) methods.

Task the model must do:
- Read a GSM8K-style math word problem.
- Produce a numeric final answer.
- For the proposed method, also emit an auditable, executable arithmetic trail (CALC) that reconstructs the solution in a constrained, Python-checkable form.

Proposed workflow (PC-L2M: Proof-Carrying Least-to-Most):
1) **Decomposition search**: sample N alternative L2M decompositions (3–6 subproblems each) via the same LLM.
2) **Proof-carrying solve**: for each decomposition, sample a solution that *must* include:
   - `CALC:` block with one assignment/expression per line, using only Python-safe arithmetic (+, -, *, /, //, %, **, parentheses) and variable references; must end with `answer = <expr>`.
   - `FINAL: <number>`.
3) **Deterministic verification (model-independent)**: a Python script parses the CALC block and safely evaluates it using an AST whitelist. A candidate is **verified** iff:
   - all CALC lines parse and evaluate without forbidden syntax,
   - referenced variables are defined,
   - `answer` is computed,
   - numeric value of `answer` matches the number in `FINAL` (tolerance 1e-6; integer canonicalization for GSM8K).
4) **Selection**:
   - discard non-verified candidates,
   - if ≥1 verified: pick verified majority answer; ties broken by simplicity (fewest CALC lines, then highest average verifier-consistency),
   - if none verified: fallback to self-consistency majority vote on extracted numeric FINAL tokens.

Comparative workflow (DV-L2M baseline):
- Same decomposition search and candidate generation budget as PC-L2M.
- Instead of Python checking, call the same LLM as a scalar “verifier” to score each candidate’s reasoning/answer; pick top-scored candidate (rubber-stamping risk).

Experiment purpose:
- Demonstrate that **external deterministic checking** (proof-carrying CALC) yields higher accuracy and better reliability diagnostics than LLM-only verification under matched sampling budgets.

Scale tuned to the provided Runner (1× NVIDIA H200 140GB VRAM, 240GB RAM):
- Use a single 8B model in bf16 with `device_map="auto"`.
- Evaluate on **GSM8K test split, first 200 items** (fast iteration) with N=5 candidates per question.
- Total generations per question:
  - PC-L2M: N decompositions + N solves (≈10 generations/question).
  - DV-L2M: N decompositions + N solves + N short verifier calls (≈15 generations/question).
- Keep `max_new_tokens` modest (decompose: 128; solve: 256; verifier: 128) to ensure runtime fits comfortably on a single H200.
- Use fixed seeds and log all intermediate artifacts (decompositions, CALC blocks, verifier scores) for reproducibility and auditing.

runner_config.description: NVIDIA H200, VRAM: 140 GB, RAM: 240 GB

evaluation_metrics.name: accuracy
evaluation_metrics.description:
**What it measures:** Exact correctness of the final numeric answer on GSM8K.

**Correctness criteria (numeric, not raw string):**
1) Extract the *first* signed number token from the model output (prefer `FINAL:` line; fallback to any number).
2) Parse gold answer from GSM8K (`answer` field after `####`).
3) Canonicalize:
   - If prediction is within 1e-6 of an integer, round to int.
   - Compare as strings for integers; otherwise compare as floats with tolerance 1e-6.
A prediction is correct if it matches the gold numeric value.

**Calculation method:**
Let N be number of evaluated problems, and I_i ∈ {0,1} indicate correctness for item i.

accuracy = (1/N) * Σ_i I_i

**Task appropriateness:** GSM8K is a single-number-answer math benchmark; numeric normalization avoids penalizing formatting differences.

**Relevant visualizations:**
- Bar chart of accuracy by method (PC-L2M vs DV-L2M).
- Bootstrap 95% confidence interval plot for the accuracy difference (Δ).

evaluation_metrics.name: verification_pass_rate
evaluation_metrics.description:
**What it measures:** How often a *generated candidate* satisfies the proof-carrying obligation (parsable + executable CALC consistent with FINAL).

**Correctness criteria:** A candidate “passes” if the Python checker:
- successfully parses CALC,
- evaluates each line under an AST whitelist,
- computes `answer`,
- and `answer` matches `FINAL` within tolerance.

**Calculation method:**
Over all candidates across all questions:
pass_rate = (# verified candidates) / (# total candidates)
Optionally also report per-question distribution.

**Task appropriateness:** This directly quantifies whether the method can elicit machine-checkable arithmetic from the LLM—critical for the proposed framework.

**Relevant visualizations:**
- Histogram of per-question number of verified candidates (0..N).
- Stacked bar: fail reasons (parse error, undefined var, mismatch FINAL, disallowed syntax).

evaluation_metrics.name: verified_coverage
evaluation_metrics.description:
**What it measures:** Fraction of questions for which *at least one* candidate is verified (i.e., the deterministic checker can be used for selection).

**Correctness criteria:** A question is “covered” if ∃ candidate j among N such that candidate j passes verification.

**Calculation method:**
coverage = (# questions with ≥1 verified candidate) / (# questions)

**Task appropriateness:** PC-L2M only provides its reliability benefits when at least one candidate satisfies the proof obligation.

**Relevant visualizations:**
- Line plot of coverage vs N (e.g., N∈{1,3,5,8}) to show scaling of coverage with search width.

evaluation_metrics.name: conditional_accuracy_given_verified
evaluation_metrics.description:
**What it measures:** Accuracy restricted to the subset of questions where PC-L2M has ≥1 verified candidate.

**Correctness criteria:** Same as `accuracy`, but computed on subset S = {i : at least one candidate verified}.

**Calculation method:**
cond_acc = (1/|S|) * Σ_{i∈S} I_i
Report also |S|.

**Task appropriateness:** Tests the hypothesis that verification is a *useful selection signal* (i.e., verified solutions are genuinely more correct).

**Relevant visualizations:**
- Two bars: unconditional accuracy vs conditional accuracy (PC-L2M).
- Scatter: per-question verified-candidate count vs correctness (binary), optionally with smoothing.

evaluation_metrics.name: avg_calc_length
evaluation_metrics.description:
**What it measures:** Average number of CALC lines among verified candidates (simplicity proxy).

**Correctness criteria:** Count non-empty, non-comment lines in CALC block after stripping whitespace.

**Calculation method:**
avg_len = (1/M) * Σ_k L_k
where M is # verified candidates and L_k is CALC-line count.

**Task appropriateness:** Shorter executable trails are easier to audit and reduce opportunities for hidden mistakes; also used as a tie-breaker in selection.

**Relevant visualizations:**
- Box/violin plot of CALC length distribution (verified candidates only).
- Correlation plot: CALC length vs candidate verification failure rate (optional).

proposed_method.description: Inference-only prompt framework: sample multiple L2M decompositions, solve each with a constrained executable CALC trail, deterministically verify CALC in Python via AST-whitelisted evaluation, and select among *verified* candidates by majority vote with simplicity tie-break. Novelty: replaces LLM self-verification with a model-independent, auditable proof obligation while remaining prompt-only (no fine-tuning, no external tools beyond Python).

comparative_methods.description: Prompt-only baseline: sample N diverse L2M decompositions and candidate solutions, then use the same LLM as a scalar verifier/judge to score each candidate’s correctness and pick the top-scored answer (LLM-only verification; prone to correlated rubber-stamping).
